newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha approves new govt, looting goes on.
newsitem.headline: Berisha approves new govt, looting goes on.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha on Wednesday approved an interim broad-based government charged with trying to end an armed rebellion in the south and organising new elections by June.
A decree broadcast on state television said Berisha had accepted the 15-member government chosen by Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, a member of the opposition Socialists appointed on Tuesday.
"After consultations with all political forces we have tried to make a government for all Albanians. I urge Albanians to keep cool heads at this difficult time," Fino said.
In Washington, the United States ordered 160 U.S. government employees and their dependents to leave Albania because of worsening instability.
About 2,000 other Americans were also urged to leave the country. Officials said Americans would leave by commercial or charter flights, with no need for a U.S. military evacuation.
Fino said he wanted talks with armed rebels who seized towns throughout southern Albania after the collapse of shady pyramid investment schemes left thousands penniless.

His comments followed appeals from Italy and Greece to meet the rebels and an announcement that a European mediation mission led by former Austrian leader Franz Vranitzky was to return to Tirana on Thursday.

In some parts of the south the rebellion appeared to have deteriorated into lawlessness, with armed gangs roaming at will through rebel-held towns, robbing motorists, terrorising women and shooting at travellers from Greece.
A rebel council running the port of Sarande said anyone caught stealing or looting would be shot, but such warnings had little affect on gangs.
A spokesman for a newly-formed rebel National Committee for Public Salvation renewed demands for Berisha's resignation and said the insurgents wanted a place at the Tirana talks.
Anti-government rebels looted weapons from a military base near the town of Elbasan, only 55 km (34 miles) from Tirana.
In the capital itself, eyewitnesses reported groups of men had entered the military academy and removed small arms.
The chief of the national guard, Sokol Mulosmani, told reporters that secret police had entered the academy and told students to go home. Arms had been removed by secret police, he told reporters.
Tirana's mayor and leaders of major political parties appeared on television to urge residents to remain calm.
Albania's exiled King Leka said he was assessing the situation hour by hour, and was prepared to return at any time if he judged the right moment had come.
"I could be in Tirana within 24 hours of a decision. But I don't want to precipitate a civil war myself." he told Reuters in an interview at his ranch-style home outside Johannesburg.
More than 40 people have died in unrest which first broke out in January in protest at the collapse of pyramid investment schemes with the savings of hundreds of thousands of Albanians.
Fino is a former mayor of Gjirokaster -- one of the largest southern towns in rebel hands.
His appointment on Tuesday was seen as a major, if tardy, concession to the opposition days after Berisha ruled out any coalition government with the Socialists.

A weekend deal between Berisha and the opposition called for an interim all-party government, new elections by June and an amnesty for rebels to hand in thousands of weapons looted from army barracks.

But as the latest talks got under way, around 100 people denouncing Berisha looted automatic weapons from the depot near the town of Elbasan. One man was slightly injured, almost certainly by a stray bullet.

State television reported two people had died of gunshot wounds in the nearby town of Cerrik. One person was reported dead in Vlore, the Adriatic port where some of the worst violence has occurred in the past month.
In northern Albania, generally spared most of the unrest, television said one person died in the town of Bajram Curri after a rampage on Tuesday through a barracks.
The defence ministry warned people to stay away from arms depots, saying they had been mined.
